title: Researching & Selecting Prospects
summary: Prepare a concise evidence-based prospect note and natural opener; preserve CRM history, ownership and contact restrictions.

scenes.title: Research earns a better first question
scenes.narration:
Prospecting research has a practical purpose: help you approach a legitimate business with a relevant, honest question. You are not trying to learn everything about the company before speaking. You are trying to avoid preventable mistakes, recognize a plausible reason to talk and distinguish what you observed from what you still need to ask.
A useful first pass can often be brief. Review the campaign direction, confirm the business and inspect a relevant public source. Look for the service offered, general location, an appropriate business contact route and a clue about the customer journey. Stop when you have enough evidence for one sensible question, not when you have collected every available detail.
The danger is turning a clue into a conclusion. A website with a contact form does not prove that inquiries are ignored. A busy location does not prove missed calls. Research gives you a hypothesis to test in conversation. In this lesson, you will build a short research note, choose an appropriate next step and write an opener that does not invent familiarity or a business problem.

scenes.title: Begin with the campaign brief
scenes.narration:
Before searching, understand the campaign you are actually working. The company may sell nationwide, but that does not mean every employee should contact every business in every location today. Your manager may define an industry, territory, service focus, assigned list or follow-up objective. Those instructions keep the work relevant and reduce duplicated effort.
If the brief says to explore quote follow-up with local service businesses, look for businesses whose process could reasonably involve quotations. Do not quietly switch to an unrelated market because it produces more search results. If the requested market is unclear or a tool has limited coverage, record the issue and ask your manager how to proceed.
A practical brief should leave you knowing whom to research, why the conversation may be relevant, which contact channels are approved and where to record the work. It does not supply a conclusion about each business. The campaign creates a starting direction; the prospect's actual answers determine whether an opportunity exists. Keep quotas, cadence and compensation tied to current management guidance rather than inventing universal Academy rules.

scenes.overlay: Use the campaign you were assigned.

scenes.title: Confirm the business identity
scenes.narration:
Start with the basic question: am I looking at the right business? Similar names, multiple locations, outdated listings and changed ownership can confuse a quick search. Confirm enough public information to avoid mixing one company's website or phone number with another company's record. A clean identity check saves time throughout the rest of the sales process.
For a fictional example, suppose you find Cedar Home Services in two different cities. Compare the location, website and public business contact details before deciding that the entries are duplicates. A shared name alone is not enough. A matching phone may be useful evidence, but the record still needs to be understood in context.
If the source is incomplete, keep the uncertainty visible. Do not fill a blank with a number from a different location merely to make the spreadsheet look complete. Record the source you used and the date of the check when appropriate. Research quality is not measured by how few empty cells remain. It is measured by whether the next person can understand which business the record represents and what still needs verification.

scenes.title: Read the customer journey
scenes.narration:
Once identity is clear, look at how a customer appears to approach the business. Does the website invite a call, a quotation request, a booking inquiry or an online purchase? Which services are described? This helps you choose a question about the working process. It does not tell you how effectively the team handles that process behind the scenes.
Imagine a fictional landscaping company with a request-a-quote page. An observation is that the page invites project details. A useful hypothesis is that the team has a process for reviewing those details and following up. A premature conclusion is that they are losing work because they need our automation. Only the first two belong in your research preparation.
Turn the observation into a neutral question: when a quote request arrives, how does your team handle the next step? That invites the owner to describe reality. If the process already works well, acknowledge it and follow the answer. The purpose of research is to make the opening relevant, not to build a case that the prospect must agree with before you have heard from them.

scenes.title: Use sources with the right amount of confidence
scenes.narration:
Public information can be useful without being complete or current. The business's own website, a public listing and a customer review may each describe something different. Treat the source according to what it can actually establish. A third-party comment is not the same as the owner confirming the current operating process.
Suppose a review says a fictional repair shop was slow to return a call last year. That may suggest a question about response handling, but it does not prove an ongoing company-wide failure. Do not open with an accusation or pretend you audited their calls. A public complaint deserves context, and your conversation should give the business room to explain.
When sources conflict, record the conflict or choose a question that resolves it. Do not select whichever version makes the strongest pitch. Keep the research note concise enough to use, with the source attached to the relevant observation. A useful note says what was seen and what needs checking. It does not turn uncertain public material into a claim about revenue, staff performance or technical readiness.

scenes.title: Look for a realistic decision-maker path
scenes.narration:
Research can help identify the likely owner of a process, but a title does not tell you everything about buying authority. An owner, manager, coordinator or department lead may each understand a different part of the workflow. You need a realistic path to the right conversation, not a guessed title that makes the CRM look qualified.
For a fictional multi-location company, the local manager may handle customer response while another team approves technology. A useful opening asks who is responsible for the process you want to understand. If the manager can explain it and introduce the appropriate person, that may be a realistic path. Do not dismiss them simply because they are not the final signer.
At the same time, do not claim you have reached a decision maker before that is established. Record the role as known, the responsibility as reported and any introduction as an actual agreed next step. Never invent a prior relationship to bypass a gatekeeper. Honest research helps you ask for the right person; it does not give you permission to manufacture familiarity or authority.

scenes.overlay: Find the owner of the process and the path forward.

scenes.title: Check the CRM before creating more work
scenes.narration:
Before adding or contacting a prospect, check the existing CRM record and the campaign's contact restrictions. Another employee may already own the business. There may be a requested callback, a prior decline, an active assessment or a do-not-contact instruction. Public availability of contact information does not override those internal facts.
The Lead Finder screens for matching phone records and certain duplicates, but automated matching is not a complete understanding of the relationship. Different formats, shared numbers and incomplete records can still require review. Search the available records and use the business context. A tool reducing duplicates does not remove the employee's responsibility to understand an existing lead.
If you find an existing record, preserve its history and follow the ownership process. Do not create a second entry to reset a restriction or take credit for work already underway. If you cannot determine who should act, ask a manager and leave the uncertainty visible. Clean research should reduce confusion for the team and respect the prospect's previous instructions, not simply increase the number of rows in the system.

scenes.title: Prioritize relevance rather than invented certainty
scenes.narration:
A useful prospecting queue balances the assigned campaign, the quality of available information and the appropriateness of the next action. A business with a plausible process to discuss may deserve a conversation. That is different from claiming it is certain to buy. Research cannot read the owner's mind or establish a need they have not described.
Compare two fictional records. One is a confirmed service business with a relevant quote process and a clear public contact route. The other has an uncertain identity and a copied note claiming guaranteed demand for AI. The first record is easier to approach responsibly, even if it contains no dramatic prediction about revenue or interest.
Use honest reasons when deciding what to work next. A requested callback may take priority because of an actual agreement. A new prospect may fit the campaign because of its services and location. An incomplete record may need verification first. Do not treat an automated label, a confidence score or a busy-looking website as proof of urgency, buying intent or qualification. Those labels can guide review; they cannot replace discovery.

scenes.title: Practice a one-minute research note
scenes.narration:
Your practice business is fictional: Cedar Landscape Studio. Its public page offers residential project quotations, lists a general office phone and says projects begin with a consultation. You have not spoken with the team. You do not know how quickly they respond, which CRM they use or whether follow-up is a problem.
Take a short research pass using only those supplied details. Write three lines: one observed fact, one clearly labeled hypothesis and one question that would test it. Do not add a revenue estimate or a claim about missed calls. Pause and write your research note. The exercise is about using limited evidence well, not inventing a richer business history.
A strong answer might record that the page invites project quotations. The hypothesis could be that someone reviews inquiries and arranges consultations. The question might ask what happens after a quotation request arrives. If your note says they need AI because their team is too busy, replace that conclusion with a question. Good research makes uncertainty specific enough to investigate. Revise the note so the next rep can tell exactly what is known and what is only a possibility.

scenes.title: Turn research into a natural opening
scenes.narration:
A researched opening should be short, relevant and honest. It should not sound like you are reading a dossier at the prospect. Use only the observation that helps explain why you are asking about a process. Then give the person room to answer. Research has done its job when the first question makes sense.
For Cedar Landscape Studio, you might say: quick reason for the call, I saw that customers can request project quotations through your site. How does your team handle the next step after a request arrives? That opening names a public observation and asks about the process. It does not claim the owner has missed opportunities or that you already know their internal systems.
Try an opening aloud in your own words. If it contains several research details before the question, remove the extras. If it says we noticed you are losing business, replace the invented conclusion. If the person corrects the observation, acknowledge the correction and adapt. The goal is a conversation, not defending your research. A calm, useful question leaves the prospect free to explain that the process works well or to describe where it becomes difficult.

scenes.title: Keep the record useful and appropriate
scenes.narration:
Research notes should help the team conduct a relevant business conversation. They should not become a collection of unrelated personal details about an owner or employee. Keep the information tied to the business process, public professional context and approved sales purpose. More detail is not automatically more useful or more appropriate.
Record the business identity, relevant source, observed process and the question to explore. Add current CRM ownership and any existing contact restriction or callback agreement. Leave unknown fields empty or explicitly unknown according to the form. If a source is outdated or uncertain, say so rather than presenting it as a confirmed current fact.
Before moving to the next record, read your note as though another rep will act on it tomorrow. Can they understand why the business fits the campaign, what was actually observed and what should happen next? Can they distinguish a possible opportunity from an established pain point? If not, revise the note. Clear research reduces duplicated work, protects accurate handoffs and helps the first conversation start with curiosity instead of a false assumption.
scenes.visual: Purposeful instructor gesture followed by progressive teaching boards, scenario examples and practice.
scenes.overlay: Keep research tied to the business purpose.

scenes.title: Your research-to-conversation routine
scenes.narration:
Use this repeatable routine: read the campaign, confirm the business, inspect a relevant public source, check the existing CRM and prepare one useful question. Keep the first pass focused. Go deeper when a real ambiguity needs resolving or a manager requests more research, not because collecting detail feels safer than beginning an appropriate conversation.
For your practical submission, create a fictional prospect note with a source observation, a labeled hypothesis, a decision-maker question and a proposed opener. Include what you still do not know. Ask Guru to challenge any claim that goes beyond the evidence. Then revise the note and opener so they would remain honest even if the business has no problem at all.
Complete the scenario quiz and save the revised exercise. Research is not qualification, and a lead record is not a customer relationship. The purpose is to earn a useful conversation. When the prospect describes the real process, their answer becomes the new evidence. Follow it, update the record accurately and decide whether a Growth Assessment is a relevant next step rather than treating the research as a verdict.

job_aid:
RESEARCH FIELD GUIDE
ROUTINE: campaign → identity → relevant public source → CRM history → one useful question.
OBSERVATION: what the source actually shows.
HYPOTHESIS: a labeled possibility to test.
QUESTION: what would resolve the uncertainty?
VERIFY: location, website and appropriate business contact; similar names may be different businesses.
RESPECT: ownership, callback agreements and contact restrictions. Automated deduplication is not a complete relationship check.
AVOID: invented missed calls, revenue claims, buying intent, familiarity and unrelated personal details.
OPENER: one relevant observation plus one neutral question.
UPDATE: accept corrections and follow the prospect’s actual answer. Research is preparation, not qualification.

questions.prompt: A website has a quote-request form. Which note is supported?
choices: They are losing quotes.
Their team is too busy.
The site invites quote requests; ask how the next step is handled.
They need our biggest automation build.
questions.explanation: The form is an observation. Response quality, staffing problems and solution size remain unknown. The useful note turns the clue into a question.

questions.prompt: Two businesses share a name in different cities. What should you do?
choices: Merge them immediately.
Compare location, website and business contact evidence before deciding.
Use whichever phone is easiest to find.
Treat both as confirmed duplicates.
questions.explanation: Identity requires context. A name alone cannot establish a duplicate, and borrowing a phone from another location can corrupt the record.

questions.prompt: An old review reports a slow callback. What is an honest use of that information?
choices: Claim an ongoing company-wide failure.
Say you audited their calls.
Promise to recover lost revenue.
Use it cautiously as a possible question about current response handling.
questions.explanation: The review has limited context and age. It does not prove current operations, a completed audit or financial losses. Ask about the process without accusing.

questions.prompt: The CRM shows a do-not-contact instruction, but a public listing has a different phone. What is appropriate?
choices: Respect the restriction and resolve the record context through the approved process.
Call the other number to bypass the restriction.
Create a fresh record.
Delete the old history.
questions.explanation: An alternate listing does not erase the relationship or restriction. Preserve history and follow the approved ownership and contact process.

questions.prompt: A local manager understands the workflow but another team approves technology. How should you record them?
choices: Confirmed final buyer.
Irrelevant contact.
Known manager with a possible path to the appropriate decision maker.
Guaranteed assessment booking.
questions.explanation: Role, process knowledge and buying authority are different. A realistic introduction path may be useful, but neither authority nor a meeting is confirmed yet.

questions.prompt: Which record is most useful to work from?
choices: Uncertain identity plus guaranteed buying intent.
Confirmed business, relevant public process, source and an honest question.
A high confidence label with no context.
A long list of unrelated personal details.
questions.explanation: Relevant evidence and a clear question support responsible prospecting. Predictions, labels and unrelated details do not establish fit or appropriate contact.

questions.prompt: The prospect corrects your researched assumption. What should you do?
choices: Defend the website interpretation.
Ignore the correction.
Continue the memorized pitch.
Acknowledge the correction and ask about the current process.
questions.explanation: The prospect supplies new evidence. Adapt rather than defending an assumption or continuing a pitch that no longer fits.

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between research and qualification?
choices: Research prepares a useful conversation; qualification requires relevant discovery and an appropriate next step.
Research proves buying intent.
A complete spreadsheet guarantees a qualified assessment.
A public phone number confirms authority.
questions.explanation: Research cannot establish need, interest, authority or a confirmed meeting by itself. It supplies a grounded starting point for discovery.

scenario.title: Research Cedar Landscape Studio
scenario.persona: FICTIONAL business: Cedar Landscape Studio. Public details: residential project quotations, general office phone, consultation as a first step. Response time, CRM and follow-up performance are unknown. Casey is an office manager who can explain the process and may identify the appropriate decision maker. Correct claims that the website proves missed opportunities. If asked honestly, explain that quote review is handled weekly and timing may be worth exploring. Do not guarantee interest or a meeting.
scenario.opening: Guru: You have a fictional public website observation. Open naturally with Casey and test one hypothesis without inventing a problem.

rubric.opening: Uses one relevant observation and a concise process question.
rubric.accuracy: Records role, unknowns and corrections honestly.
rubric.ethics: Does not fabricate familiarity, research or results.
